en: Preface to the *Brief Commentary and Sub-commentary on the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment Definitive Meaning*,
composed by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Cūtang Monastery on Mount Zhongnan during the Tang Dynasty;
annotated by the Śramaṇa Ruyuan of Longsha Zhangjiang Chan Monastery.

The Chan Master’s name was Zongmi; he was a native of Guozhou in Xichuan. A scholar of Confucianism who passed the jinshi examinations, he was once studying at the school in Suizhou when the Venerable Daoyuan arrived from Chengdu.
Through the convergence of karmic conditions, he then paid homage to Chan Master Yuan, whereupon he left the household life and shaved his head.

"Originality, capacity for fulfillment, advantage, and constancy are the virtues of Qian (Heaven). Beginning with the single breath, 'eternal joy, self, and purity' are the virtues of the Buddha, rooted in the One Mind.

"Originality" means the beginning; "capacity for fulfillment" means penetration; "advantage" means harmony; and "constancy" means rectitude. These are the four virtues of Qian. Their beginning in the single breath is precisely the primordial breath (*yuanqi*) that is the fundamental source of heaven and earth.

First, Confucian learning is cited to reveal the principle of ultimate awakening; thus it says, "eternal joy, self, and purity. "Eternal" means not subject to change; "joy" refers to the path out of suffering; "self" is that upon which the sages rely; and "purity" means being free from defilement. These are the four virtues of the Buddha, rooted in the One Mind.

The single mind is precisely the wondrous mind of the fundamental enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) of all Buddhas. By concentrating the vital energy (*prāṇa*), one attains pliancy; by cultivating the single mind, one achieves the Way.

(By skillfully maintaining the vital energy, one responds to things with flexibility and compliance; by refining and clarifying the single mind, there is no aspect of the Way that is not complete. As for this mind: it is profound, empty, wondrous, and pure; it is brilliantly radiant and spiritually luminous. It neither goes nor comes, darkly penetrating the three periods of time.

Neither central nor peripheral, it penetrates through the ten directions. (Pervading vertically and horizontally, it is solely this single mind; how could it be characterized by going and coming, or by center and periphery?)
[How could there be such a thing? Since it is neither extinguished nor born, how could the four mountains [of birth, old age, sickness, and death] cause harm?

Since it is detached from both nature and characteristics, how could the five colors blind one? (The "four mountains" refer to birth, old age, sickness, and death. When arising and ceasing are exhausted, all Buddhas appear before one; what thing could possibly cause harm? When both nature and characteristics are simultaneously detached, there is truly not a single dharma that can confront the mind;

how then could the five colors blind right vision? Dwelling within the stream of birth and death, the black pearl shines alone amidst the vast blue sea. (This refers to the Bodhisattva’s compassionate vow to deliver sentient beings: True Suchness is not obscured, and one skillfully enters into birth...)

Because death has been transcended, one is able to manifest illumination like the pearl beneath the chin of a black dragon, shining alone amidst the vast blue ocean; seated upon the shore of Nirvana, the crescent moon is solitary and bright against the azure sky.

(This refers to the eternally abiding four noble truths and the self-nature purity of *nirvāṇa*, which, like the solitary brilliance of the bright moon in the azure sky, transcends to the other shore.

How magnificent is the source from which the myriad dharmas arise! The myriad dharmas are illusory, arising through the convergence of conditions. (The *Book of Changes* says: "How great is the Primordial Qian! All things derive their beginning from it. This clarifies that the initial manifestation of the myriad dharmas depends upon the mutual support of the One Mind.

Since dharmas are fundamentally unreal and are all produced through the conjunction of external conditions, the treatise states: "There is not a single dharma that does not arise from causes and conditions. The dharmas that arise are fundamentally non-existent; everything is merely...
Consciousness cognizes like a phantom or a dream; it is but a single mind. When the mind is stilled and yet knows, this is called Perfect Enlightenment (*yuanjue*).

It is all-pervasive, pure, and within it there is no room for anything else. (This clarifies that phenomena arise from the dust of consciousness; since that which is produced is unreal, it is called a phantom or a dream. If one can remain still while constantly illuminating, then the function of illumination is boundless, hence it is called "all-pervasive.

As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "It is untainted and pure; how could anything else be further contained therein? Therefore, its virtuous functions are boundless, yet they are all of one single nature, arising from that very nature.
When the characteristics of objects and cognition are clearly distinct yet their natures are fused, and body and mind are vast and open, this is compared to the Ocean Seal (Sāgarāmudrā).
It transcends the great void—vast and brilliant, far beyond the reach of thought and deliberation. (Its virtuous function flourishes and manifests, with boundless wondrous responses;

thus, objects, characteristics, body, and mind are simultaneously and utterly transparent, like a sea stilled and still. Because one may approach it through any single dharma, it exceeds the great void and the realm of thought and deliberation. Our Buddha realized this and took pity on sentient beings who are deluded.

Twice he sighed in wonder at how marvelous it was; thrice he contemplated this great matter. (The "Chapter on the Manifestation" in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "O Son of the Buddha, how marvelous! Not a single sentient being lacks the wisdom of the Tathāgata;

yet because of deluded thoughts and attachments, they do not realize it. Thus, for three weeks, the Buddha contemplated that for the sake of these great causal conditions, he had appeared in the world.

Having fully perfected the Ten Powers, he was able to crush the demonic armies beneath the Bodhi tree (when the Buddha first attained enlightenment, he subdued the demonic hosts at the Bodhi tree). Thereupon, he gave rise to the Four Minds, desiring to reveal the treasure within the house.

Treasury. (Arising these four minds—compassion, pity, joy, and equanimity—to point out the precious treasury within each person's own home. Yet, losing one’s head and abandoning one’s father is easy to do, whereas awakening to it is difficult.

(The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says that when Yaśoda saw his face in a mirror, he became enraged at his own head for not seeing its features and ran about in a frenzy; the *Lotus Sūtra* says the impoverished son abandoned his father and fled. As for Yaśoda, once his madness subsided of its own accord, that very subsiding was Bodhi—this is the ease of awakening.

As for the impoverished son returning home, his inferior mindset still persisted, so he was first made to remove filth—this is the difficulty of awakening. Therefore, in the Immortal Garden and the Site of Enlightenment, the teachings arose as sudden and gradual. (The Buddha, regarding...)

In the Deer Park, the ancient abode of seers, the names of the Four Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination were taught; this is called the Gradual Teaching (*ānupūrvika-śāsana*). In the *araṇya* and the Bodhimanda, the *Avataṃsaka* was taught; this is called the Sudden Teaching (*tadaṅga-śāsana*). The gradual approach establishes five distinct periods in which emptiness and existence manifest alternately. The sudden approach possesses no differentiation between the two truths, for its profound essence is beyond all relative dependence. Is this present sutra not of the same category as the Sudden Teaching? [The first period: After the Buddha attained enlightenment, he taught the *Āgama* and other sutras of the Lesser Vehicle; these are called the teachings of the Sarvāstivāda school. [The second period: He refuted the grasping of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and spoke exclusively of the *Prajñā*; these are called the teachings of the Emptiness school. [The third period: He taught that while objects are empty, the mind exists. (These three periods represent the gradual teaching. The fourth period is the teaching of the One Vehicle, and the fifth period is the teaching of the *Saṃdhinirmocana*. The *Saṃdhinirmocana* and other sutras are called the "Teaching of the Middle Way," wherein the provisional teachings of the four periods of assembly lead into the reality of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, which is termed the "Teaching of the Common Return. At the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* assembly, it directly points out that all sentient beings will certainly become Buddhas; this is termed the "Teaching of Eternal Abiding. Regarding the gradual differences:

within the preceding teachings on emptiness and existence, the two truths of the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) were already clarified through their alternating manifestation. Now, however, one enters the *dhyāna* contemplation of "neither of the two" (neither existence nor emptiness) all at once. Because the profound, subtle, and wondrous mind transcends the dharmas of dualistic opposition, the Buddha classifies this as the "Sudden Teaching" of the Mahāyāna.

Thus, when the Tathāgata enters the Land of Tranquil Light, the ordinary and the sagely share a single source, and the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) manifests with its retinue of principal and attendant figures in perfect unity.

Assembly. (The Buddha enters the Great Treasury of Radiance, which is the ground of the pure awakening of sentient beings; he manifests the supreme response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and dwells together with the twelve great beings in an assembly of the equal Dharma, hence it is called "Principal and Retinue").
The Great Being Mañjuśrī first inquires into the cause of the original arising, and the Bhagavat first proclaims the ultimate fruit.

(This refers to the fruit of ultimate realization, namely the Unsurpassed Dharma King who possesses a *dhāraṇī* gate named Perfect Enlightenment [*Samantabhadra-vimala-bodhi*]. Mañjuśrī is a transcription of the Sanskrit for "Wen-shu," and Bhagavat is the Sanskrit for "Shi-zun" [World-Honored One]). Illuminating this true essence:

When those dream-forms are extinguished, one knows there is no self and no person; who then undergoes saṃsāra? (Reflecting on this pure state of awakening, one realizes that ignorance is not real, just as a person in a dream finds nothing upon waking;

therefore it is called "extinguishing. To fully know there is no self and no person, who else could undergo birth and death? All manner of illusory transformations arise within the awakened mind; when the illusions are exhausted, awakening is perfected, the mind penetrates all, and the Dharma is pervasive.

(To leave illusion is to attain awakening, whereby one immediately gains unconditioned purity; thus it is said the mind penetrates everywhere, even to the point that the gates of dhāraṇī fill the entire Dharma-realm.)

Therefore it is said that the Dharma is all-pervasive. The mind is originally Buddha, yet due to the arising of thought, it drifts and sinks; though the shore does not actually move, it appears to rush past because of the movement of the boat (see the note in this scripture).
Sudden removal of the false ruler means emptiness does not produce flowers; gradual exhaustion of the source of craving means gold is no longer encased in ore.

If one can suddenly eliminate that which takes delusion and illusion as its own master, then the flower will vanish from the void and the root of craving shall be severed at its source; it will naturally become gradually purified, like ore becoming gold that never again turns back into ore. When principle transcends cultivation and realization, wisdom appears as if having gradations, yet the realization of each preceding error is what constitutes each succeeding stage.
How much more so for one whose virtue is equal and perfectly luminous, such that delusions are forgotten and arising and ceasing are absent!

If the ultimate truth did not require cultivation, yet one were to give rise to wisdom, sever delusions, and seek realization, this would indicate a failure to reach the equality of self-nature and a manifestation of differentiation. If one awakens to the errors of the past, then the future fruit will be revealed.

How much more so for one who has realized the forgetting of the delusions of arising and ceasing—this is indeed the perfectly luminous state. Nevertheless, a fine horse already in the stable stirs at the shadow of the whip (those of the highest capacity enter awakening without relying on expedient means, like a fine horse that proceeds upon seeing the shadow of the whip).

A great treasure buried in dust requires the application of a method of treatment (sentient beings who have turned their backs on awakening do not know that their own jewel is buried within the dust of afflictions;

they must rely on the methods of cultivation and treatment). Therefore, when the three contemplations are clarified and purified, both the provisional and the real are entered. Entering Perfect Enlightenment is not by a single path; according to the differences in one's nature, there should be three [approaches].

The "types" refer to both the true and the provisional. Entering the True means merging with phenomena to clarify the spirit; this contemplation is *śamatha*. Entering the Provisional means giving rise to illusions to dissolve defilements; this contemplation is *samāpatti*. Entering Both means that which is neither true nor provisional, yet both true and provisional;

this is the contemplation of the absolute, numinous mind, which is *dhyāna* (as explained in the Commentary). These various wheels are interwoven, practiced either singly, in pairs, or in combination.

Although the *Awakening of Mahāyāna* is fundamentally beyond cultivation, because sentient beings rely on non-awakening, they employ the power of illusion to practice twenty-five kinds of pure wheels. This crushes and grinds away karmic afflictions, like the intermingling of five-colored threads in brocade. One may practice the first three contemplations singly, or practice the twenty-one contemplations in combination.

Because one practices the single, the multiple, and the perfect through the interweaving and overlapping of circular cultivation and the subsequent unification of these views, it is called "single, multiple, and perfect cultivation. The four phases [of illness] lie latent within the spirit; they are not perceived and thus offer resistance.

The four illnesses emerge from their substance as the mind-flower manifests its brilliance. (The self, persons, sentient beings, and life-span dwell latently within the *ālayavijñāna*; because of this, one cannot enter awakening, and the nature of awakening acts as a barrier, obstructing all who would enter.

The four illnesses are: acting, ceasing, relying, and extinguishing. Furthermore, one establishes long, medium, and short periods [of practice] (see the note in this scripture). One applies the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) by maintaining mindfulness and gathering the mind. During the three periods, one maintains right mindfulness and performs repentance.

It is said: "If one is able to maintain mindfulness, after twenty-one days, if one no longer performs repentance but instead single-mindedly collects the mind to again cultivate the three contemplations, this constitutes the preparatory practice (*prayoga*). By practicing these individually, collectively, and alternately, the karmic obstacles and the obstacles of delusion will be extinguished.
One will achieve the body of wisdom, and as stillness reaches its ultimate limit, awakening will pervade hundreds of thousands of worlds, and the realm of the Buddhas will manifest before one.

After the three periods, one should practice the three contemplations individually; that which has not been heard of previously must never be grasped. 'Collective practice' means practicing all three types together. 'Alternating practice' means that if one contemplation has not yet been mastered, one returns to practice another. By means of this, all obstacles are eliminated, and through gradual cultivation and realization, [enlightenment] is achieved."

This is because the body of wisdom is profoundly tranquil and its awakening is all-pervasive, extending from a single body to hundreds of thousands of worlds. Therefore, hearing these five names surpasses the merit of giving away lands and jewels;

explaining the meaning of even half a verse of this sutra excels the merit of [giving to] sentient beings as numerous as the sands of a hundred Ganges Rivers who have attained the fruit of Arhatship through the Hinayana.

This is truly because there is no dharma that is not upheld and no capacity that is not reached. (The name of this sutra is *Vaipulya*. If one can hear and uphold these five names, it is more excellent than piling up treasures and distributing them as gifts to sentient beings as numerous as the sands of a hundred Ganges Rivers to enable them to attain the fruit of Arhatship; it is not equal to proclaiming even half a verse of this sutra.)

The *dhāraṇī* gates can universally sustain the sudden and gradual methods of cultivation, skillfully adapting to the three types of faculties without failing to encompass them all. Alas! The "Ba-song" (Barbarian song) has many harmonizers, while the "Yang-chun" (Springtime) is rarely matched;

the "Xue-qu" (Snow Song) is seldom responded to, and the definitive meaning remains hidden within the Dragon Treasury. As the song of Yingzhong says: "The 'Ba-song' is a lowly tune, yet those who harmonize with it are numerous. This is a metaphor for how the Lesser Vehicle is easy to follow;

in this teaching, taking awakening to one's nature as the true direct cognition (*pratyakṣa*), and seeking awakening as the inferential cognition (*anumāna*). The dharma realized through inferential cognition, when possessed by a mind of direct cognition, is consistently called "remote," like a monkey’s heart leaping—now up, now down. The "Yang-chun" [is likewise rare].

The name of the "High Melody of the White Snow" was such that those who could harmonize with it were exceedingly few; likewise, the lectures on the Mahāyāna were so rare that those who could respond to them were scarce, resulting in the teachings of definitive meaning becoming hidden away within the dragon-treasury (the canon).

Zongmi, while still a youth, specialized in the *Luo Gao* (the Classics of Lu), and upon reaching adulthood, he investigated the *Zhu Fen* (the texts from Zhu, i.e., India); yet he remained submerged in the traps and snares [of words], tasting only the dregs. "At the time I tied up my hair, I studied the *Gao* of Zhongni of the state of Lu;

after reaching the age of twenty, I researched the texts of Gautama from the land of Zhu. Now, being doubly deluded regarding the books of both Lu and Zhu, I have failed to obtain the fish or the rabbit, and am merely submerged in the traps and snares. When Duke Huan of Qi was reading in his study hall, a wheelwright passing by said to him: "What you, sir, are reading is ancient..."

People are like dregs, meaning they do not obtain the flavor of true essence. Fortunately, at Fu (the *fu* sound is pronounced like *fú*; located on the west bank of the Fu River in Suizhou), when the Master was twenty-five years old, he visited Daoyuan and inquired about the Dharma;
their minds were in accord, like a mustard seed meeting the point of a needle. As for the encounter with Chan in the Southern School and the meeting with this scripture, see the preceding preface.

With a single word, the ground of his mind was opened; within a single scroll, the heavens of meaning shone brightly. (When the Master first received the scripture and reached the "Universal Eye" chapter in the first fascicle, he profoundly awakened to the passage on the extinction of illusions and so forth;

it can be said that the principles of truth were already clarified within this single scroll. How much more so, then, having received the seal of approval from a single word of his original teacher, from this point forward he has unlocked the key and opened his heart, such that the Dharma pervades his mind.

There is no doubt that he will greatly propagate the Perfect Teaching. Recently, [realizing] that the Way is not a fixed way and that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, I now know for certain that the mind is the Buddha-mind.

"One shall become a Buddha. (Previously, he had regarded the study of the "trap" [the scriptures] as not being the True, Constant, and Unchanging Way, but rather as the practice of impermanence, arising, and ceasing; now, having realized the false to reveal the True, he understood that "this very mind is Buddha").

However, because the Buddha is called the One of All-Knowledge (*sarvajñā*), the cultivation of this wisdom must rely upon extensive learning; thus, he again traveled to a hundred cities to sit and explore the various scriptures. (The Buddha is called the One of All-Knowledge;

to cultivate this wisdom, one must rely on extensive learning, the intent being to broadly support one's hearing and vision, just as Sudhana visited over a hundred cities to universally consult spiritual friends. Consequently, he went to pay his respects to Chan Master Weizhong of Jingnan. Zhong said, "You are a person who transmits the teachings.")

"It would be appropriate to lead [the teachings] to the imperial capital. He then met Master Zhao of Luoyang, who said, "This man is a bodhisattva; he will be a great benefit as my friend. Following this, they traveled on to seek instruction from one another before finally settling at Mount Zhongnan.

Together with Zhiju and others, they vowed not to descend the mountain for three years, during which time they exhaustively examined the Tripiṭaka and spent their days seated in the study of various scriptures. Although their lecturing was extensive, their learning was modeled after that of Master An. Formerly, there was Dharma Master Tai of Pucheng who would lecture without first listening to the texts.

Consequently, Guifeng Xiangyang was able to obtain the National Teacher Qingliang’s commentaries on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. Delighted by what he had encountered, Xiangyang never practiced formal listening; he lectured upon them after reading them only once. In the fifth year of the Yuanhe era, he went to Xiangyang and lectured on them for the first time; subsequently, he proceeded to the Eastern Capital (Luoyang).

I once again open this Dharma assembly, feeling ashamed that my worth differs from that of the wise; thus I say I am unworthy to occupy the seat of Tai [Dao’an] of Xiangyang, who was a master of his generation. All people said, "If one does not take Dao’an as a teacher in study, one’s principles will not pass the test.

Having received your grace, I feel like a deluded disciple receiving the seal of approval from a true son of the Buddha. While lecturing in the Eastern Capital, a disciple named Tai Gong severed his arm to celebrate the Dharma. The Imperial Resident submitted a formal petition inquiring whether there were indeed such lectures on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* under the guidance of the Master.

At that time, Guifeng had not yet seen the commentaries of Qingliang (Zongmi); fearing he might fail to receive proper recognition, he sent a messenger with a letter to pay respects from afar as a disciple. The letter stated that the lecture was not undertaken lightly, but was based on genuine realization, and so forth.

In his reply, Qingliang wrote: "Having received your instructions on the essential purport of the teachings, my heart is filled with profound sorrow. Since I began lecturing, I have sometimes spoken face-to-face and others have received it in their hearts; these have been transmitted and spread until they fill foreign lands.

Yet, even when Boya snapped his strings and Zhongni tilted his carriage, they still relied upon form and sound. How much more so when transmitting meaning without meeting in person—is this not something that has never occurred in my own mind? Unless one relies on the power of the Sage, one must surely depend on past causes; you should comfort yourself in this regard. You may be compared to the true son of a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin).

If you were to meet me once more, what further could be added to the liberation already established within you? As for the 'true son,' this refers to a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage of the *Avataṃsaka* who receives his position, comparable to the thousand sons of a Wheel-Turning King; only one born of the principal queen is eligible to receive the consecration. [The phrase] "Meeting again a close friend" [is noted].

I am deeply moved by the Buddha’s kindness and have long lamented my own solitude and poverty; now I shall present this Dharma-gift. (The *Lotus Sūtra* says: "For example, there was a person who went to the house of a close friend, who pointed out a jewel sewn in his garment, which he could always use as he wished.

The "close friend" is the Buddha. Thus, Master Yuan said: "In this sūtra, the Buddhas entrust it to you," and the transmission from various masters is all metaphorically likened to a close friend. Guifeng said: "Observing current events, one can verify past causes;

one certainly knows that in a previous life one received compassionate instruction, and hearing it again today is why it is called 'repeated. From this, one knows how to repay kindness. One constantly laments being a way-seeking student who benefits others with no Dharma-wealth to provide for them—is this not indeed being solitary and poor? Now I shall present this gift of livelihood.)

[The following works] are titled "Collected Teachings" (*Miaojiao*). He compiled the *Prajñāpāramitā*, wove together the *Avataṃsaka*, and extracted the essentials of the *Vinaya* to elucidate the *Vijñaptimātratā*.

In the fourteenth year of the Yuanhe era, at Xingfu Temple, he collected the two treatises of Asaṅga and Vasubandhu, along with the commentaries and annotations of Master Sengzhao, to compile a sub-commentary and an abridgment of the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.

In the second year of the Changqing era, at Fengde Temple, he selected the essential passages from the Great Commentary on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, arranged them in sequence, and codified them into five fascicles, entitled *Huayan Lunianguan* (The Weaving of the Avataṃsaka). Regarding the five divisions of the *Vinaya*, as their terminology is verbose and their meanings expansive, they are difficult to consult for practical application; thus, he extracted and compiled those portions most suitable for use.

The collected writings comprise three fascicles; he composed the *Commentary on the Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Vimsatikā) in two fascicles at Deyou Monastery in the Capital, hence it is said that [this work] "elucidates and reveals" [the meaning].

It is accompanied by the *Awakening of Faith* (*Yuánjué*). (The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* exists in upper, middle, and lower versions, each containing countless verses and chapters; while scriptures such as the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* refer to it as the "Flower Ornament" [*Huáhuá*], if one seeks to directly point to the wondrous, ultimate essence, nothing is as suited for those of the highest capacity as the *Awakening of Faith*, which allows for immediate entry into the Buddha-realm.
Therefore, I have thoroughly examined various treatises and repeatedly studied the works of a hundred schools to sharpen my faculties before composing this commentary.

(First, I clarified the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*; subsequently, I consulted Master Wéiquò’s one-fascicle commentary from Bǎoguó Monastery, Master Wùshí’s two-fascicle commentary from Xiāntiān Monastery, and Master Jiānzhì’s commentary from Jiànfú Monastery.)

The Master’s commentary consists of four fascicles; the commentary by Dharma Master Daoshuan of Haizang Monastery consists of three fascicles. Through repeated investigation and exhaustive analysis, they mutually clarify strengths and weaknesses. As it is said, "If one desires to excel in a task, one must first sharpen one's tools" before proceeding with the exegesis.

With a mind attuned to the sacred intent, he applied his utmost thought and refined his study until the meaning was fully realized. Encompassing both the *dharmatā* (nature) and *lakṣaṇa* (characteristics) schools, and integrating both the gradual and sudden approaches of Chan, he codified these into three fascicles (*Dashu*).

This was transmitted for those of strenuous learning. [He] attained a profound resonance with the true mind, achieving perfect alignment with the sacred intent. Furthermore, he was able to exhaust his divine contemplation to investigate the essential points, such that the appropriate meanings were complete within the two traditions of *dharmatā* and *lakṣaṇa*, and the gate of *dhyāna* integrated both the sudden and gradual paths.

The two teachings were compiled to form the *Great Commentary* (*Daisho*), which extensively expounds the Dharma and its meaning for transmission to those of superior faculties and strong learning, so that the seeds of wisdom may circulate without end.

However, because the faculties, desires, and natures of those in the upper, middle, and lower grades differ, I have taken that Dharma and adapted it to suit them; following what is easy and simple, I have further extracted the essential points and directly annotated the root sutra.

Those of superior faculties desire breadth but weary of brevity, while those of middle faculties find the balance between the broad and the concise; those of inferior faculties can be understood by extension. Since their fundamental natures differ, I have encompassed all according to their capacities. Now, taking the principles of Heaven and Earth—simplicity and ease—as my model, I have produced this abbreviated commentary.

The principle by which all things are accomplished through detailed development is that Qian acts with ease to know, while Kun acts with simplicity to function; thus, the great creation and transformation both proceed from ease and simplicity, each attaining its own appropriateness.

Therefore, Guifeng once again extracted the essential passages from his *Guangshu* (Extensive Commentary) and provided direct annotations beneath the original text, producing the *Lieshu* (Abridged Commentary) in two fascicles—so named because it serves as a counterpart to the extensive version. This is intended for those who would "accord with phenomena and accord with mind," such that they might daily increase [in virtue] and daily diminish [in attachment].

(Those who have learning but no realization of the Way accord with phenomena; those who have realization of the Way but no learning accord with mind. When the mind that accords with phenomena is daily diminished, the myriad practices are harmonized; when the phenomena that accord with mind are daily diminished...)

To benefit from [the teachings] so that the thousand sages may return to the same path, one must strive to incorporate both reduction and augmentation in the study of learning and the Way. Although my own scholarly pursuits have been neglected and overgrown, I have roughly clarified the intent of Guifeng.

If one can swim beyond the realms of reduction and augmentation and look up and down amidst the inquiries of the Way and Learning, then one who shares in attainment has never truly attained it, and one who shares in loss has never truly lost it. Being able to forget what is shared between gain and loss, I am likewise one for whom the cultural tradition has not yet perished.
